newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila opens reverse repo deals to tax examination.
newsitem.headline: Manila opens reverse repo deals to tax examination.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank said on Monday it had opened all primary transactions in termed reverse repos to examination by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR).

Central Bank treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters the bank, which reopened its termed reverse repos on Monday after closing them on Thursday, had attached a condition under which reverse repo buyers would waive their right to secrecy.
The Central Bank's new condition will enable authorities to overcome a provision in the Philippines' bank secrecy law which give banks the right not to reveal any of their transactions.

"The move is to assist the BIR in tracking the transactions between the Central Bank and the banks ... So every time the BIR wants to look at the transactions, we can furnish it with the transactions without asking permission from the banks," Edeza said.

The measure was imposed by the Central Bank to help the government collect more tax. The finance department recently said it had lost about 2.0 billion pesos as some banks had not remitted income tax on interest from reverse repo transactions.
Edeza said the new reverse repos also carried a reminder that their incomes were covered by the 35 percent corporate tax.
"We are just putting that on record. If they do pay taxes on these instruments, then they don't have to worry about the tax payment," he added.

Edeza said that the tax would not be collected in advance. Traders had earlier told Reuters that many banks had stayed away from the reverse repo window on Monday morning in the belief that the new conditions included payment of advance tax.
The Central Bank offered on Monday one-month reverse repos at 11.25 percent, two-month reverse repos at 11.375 percent, and three-month reverse repos at 11.5 percent.
These reverse repos are tradeable in the secondary market and sold to institutional investors.
